result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.get_edge()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Get an edge object by an edge ID. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L6468-L6556){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.get_edge(edge_id) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Get edge](/assets/graphs/get-edge.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The shared four-node graph with node ids in pills and edge ids on the edges. The queried edge 3, between B and C, is in the accent color, as are the ids 2 and 3 of its endpoints. The card returns the Edge object Edge(id=3, 2 -> 3)." width="100%"} Retrieves the `Edge` object for the specified edge ID. The `Edge` object has five properties: - `id`: the integer edge ID - `source` and `target`: the integer node IDs of the endpoints (not their labels) - `weight`: the edge weight as a float, or `None` if no `weight=` was given when the edge was added - `attributes`: a dict of the edge's other attributes (such as `rel` or `type`), or `None` if it has none Use it to inspect everything stored on one edge, e.g. after finding its ID with `find_edge_ids()` or `get_edge_ids()`. If you only need the endpoints, `get_node_ids_by_edge_id()` returns them directly; to see all edges at once, use `get_edge_df()`. In an undirected graph, `source` and `target` simply record the order in which the endpoints were given to `add_edge()`. As with `get_node()`, the `attributes` dict is not a copy: changing it changes the attributes stored in the graph, so treat it as read-only. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [edge_id]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The integer ID of the edge to retrieve. Edge IDs are assigned automatically, starting at `1`, in the order edges are added. An ID that doesn't exist returns `None`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Edge | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `Edge` object, or `None` if no edge has that ID. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} `get_edge()` looks up an edge by its ID and returns the underlying `Edge` object, whose `source`/`target` are resolved node IDs rather than the original labels: ::: {#e2f0365b .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_node(label="A") .add_node(label="B") .add_edge("A", "B", weight=1.5, type="friend") ) edge_ids = graph.get_edge_ids() edge = graph.get_edge(edge_ids[0]) edge.source, edge.target ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (1, 2) ``` ::: ::: `weight` and `attributes` are also available directly on the edge. The weight is kept separately, so `attributes` holds only the remaining keyword arguments: ::: {#a02e0f6b .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} edge.weight, edge.attributes ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (1.5, {'type': 'friend'}) ``` ::: ::: A common pattern is to find an edge's ID from its endpoints with `find_edge_ids()` and then fetch the full edge. Here the edge was added as `"C"` to `"B"`, which is the orientation the `Edge` object reports (`3 -> 2`): ::: {#050057d7 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("C", "B", {"rel": "road"})]) ) edge_id = graph.find_edge_ids("B", "C")[0] graph.get_edge(edge_id) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` Edge(id=2, 3 -> 2) ``` ::: ::: An edge ID that doesn't exist returns `None` rather than raising: ::: {#77668bdd .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.get_edge(99) is None ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` True ``` ::: :::
